summary:
Delta-V Tycoon is a free browser game in which players, alone or as an online crew of up to four, design and fly a complete space mission. Real missions are chains of trade-offs: one more instrument adds science, but also mass, power, data and cost, which ripple into the battery, the radio
and the rocket. Students rarely get to feel those connections. In Delta-V Tycoon they pick one of five missions inspired by real ones (from watching Nile Delta farms to relaying data for Mars rovers), split a budget between four crew roles, and build the spacecraft part by part while seven live meters track
mass, power, budget, data, comms, time and delta-v. A GO/NO-GO readiness review built on NASA JPL's Concept Maturity Levels explains every problem in plain words. Then they launch, handle surprises such as solar storms and dust storms, and get a report that explains why the mission succeeded or failed, what to fix next, and which real mission their design resembles. It answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning NASA's own mission design process into a game anyone can learn in minutes
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Delta-V Tycoon is a free browser game (no install, no account) in which players, alone or as an online crew of up to four, design and fly a complete space mission: https://megumiinuwu.github.io/Delta-V-Tycoon/

It follows NASA's own mission process in six phases:

1. Need & Goals: pick one of five missions inspired by real ones (Eyes on the Nile: crop and water monitoring for Egypt; Storm Watcher: weather from geostationary orbit; Ice Hunter: water ice on the Moon; Red Relay: Mars atmosphere science plus rover data relay; First Light: an infrared telescope at L2) and hear a voiced briefing with the requirements, budget, launch window and "who uses your data".

2. Concept: in team mode the four crew roles (Mission Commander, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, Communications & Data Officer) must all agree on how to split the budget.

3. Requirements & Design: each role builds its part of the spacecraft while seven live meters (mass, power, budget, data, comms, time, delta-v) update. They use real relationships, simplified for play: the rocket equation, the power and eclipse battery budget, the link budget and ground-station contact time, pointing accuracy, light delay, launch windows and debris disposal rules. A Trade-Space Explorer plots science against cost for any one choice.

4. Build & Verify: a GO/NO-GO readiness review of 25 checks, built on NASA JPL's Concept Maturity Levels, explains every problem in plain words and has a "Fix" button that jumps to the part to change. Then comes an animated launch that can fail based on rocket reliability.

5. Implement: the mission is simulated day by day. Ten kinds of events (solar storms, Martian dust storms, reaction-wheel failures, budget cuts, discoveries...) ask the responsible role for a decision, and the options depend on what you built.

6. Results: stars, a score out of 1000, a "Why" lesson for every problem, one-click "Apply & retry" fixes, a comparison of every attempt, and a Mission Twin: the real mission your design resembles.

Try it: Play Solo, pick "Eyes on the Nile" (Cadet) and press Start. For a hard mission, enter the challenge code DVT-red_relay-director-i (Red Relay at Mars, Flight Director).

BENEFITS

- Players feel the chain of trade-offs behind every real mission: one more instrument means more mass, power, data and cost, which ripple into the battery, the radio and the rocket.

- Every failure is explained, so players learn from it instead of guessing.

- It is free and runs in any laptop or desktop browser, so a school lab can use it at once; online rooms let a class play in teams of four.

- Players practise teamwork and negotiation, because each role's goal pulls against the others.

- The Mission Academy logs 33 space concepts (delta-v, eclipse, light delay, link budget...) as players meet them, and "?" buttons explain any term in place.

INTENDED IMPACT

- Make mission design approachable for school and university students who never had access to it. A teacher can give the whole class one challenge code and compare results fairly.

- Connect space to people's needs: Eyes on the Nile ties a satellite to water and food in Egypt, and every mission says who uses its data.

- Inspire the next space engineers in Egypt and beyond by letting them run a mission from idea to results in 10–20 minutes.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Zustand, Firebase Realtime Database (online rooms, chat, leaderboard), Recharts, lz-string and Vitest, hosted on GitHub Pages. Python with Pillow and NumPy for our procedural pixel art, ffmpeg for audio, and Kokoro-82M text-to-speech for the character voices (AI-generated speech, disclosed). Claude Code was used as a coding assistant (disclosed). No special hardware is needed. Code: https://github.com/MegumiinUwU/Delta-V-Tycoon

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- A real NASA method becomes the game itself: the six mission phases are the game's steps, and the Concept Maturity meter turns "is my design ready?" into a visible goal.

- Failure is part of the game: you may launch with NO-GO items, and the report shows exactly why things went wrong and how to fix them.

- Decisions depend on the design. At Mars, signals take 12.5 minutes, so during a solar storm "enter safe mode" is only possible if you built in an onboard computer that can act alone.

- The Mission Twin reveal links the player's design to a real mission such as Landsat 9, MAVEN or the James Webb Space Telescope.

- Multiplayer roles match NASA's launch, space and ground segments, with a budget council and a "tycoon" economy where money left over raises the score.

- Challenge codes give every team the same surprises for fair competitions, and the online leaderboard verifies scores by replaying the mission.

- A voiced crew, original pixel art and synthesised chiptune music make it feel like a real game, not a worksheet.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific validity and playability: real formulas with simplified values, every source cited, and options that cannot work always say why.

- Learning curve: three difficulties (Cadet with hints, Engineer, Flight Director), plain language, a glossary and a 2-minute first mission.

- Fairness and replay: seeded events, challenge codes and replay-verified scores.

- Access: no install or login, solo or online play, built to run smoothly on ordinary laptops.

- Teamwork: four roles whose goals conflict on purpose, so the team must negotiate.

- Honesty and credit: all NASA and partner sources, open-source tools and AI use are disclosed; no agency logos are used.

- Local relevance: a mission about the Nile Delta, alongside Moon, Mars and deep-space missions.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

Numbers are simplified game values, not engineering-grade. The game is designed for laptop and desktop browsers, and the voices are in English only. Next: more missions (asteroid, Europa), Arabic and other languages, and a teacher mode with class challenges and results.
